question: What is the primary goal of the Drug Revolving Fund pricing model in public health facilities?

options.A: To generate high profits for the hospital management
options.B: To subsidize private pharmaceutical companies operating in rural areas
options.C: To provide all medications completely free of charge to patients
options.D: To ensure a constant supply of essential medicines through cost recovery

explanation: The DRF relies on continuous cost recovery to replace sold inventory and maintain medicine stocks. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T5#GNS215_U3_T5_h1)

question: Why does DRF pricing differ fundamentally from commercial retail pharmacy pricing?

options.A: Commercial pharmacies receive direct funding from international donors.
options.B: Commercial pharmacies sell only expired or near-expiry medicines.
options.C: DRF pricing aims for cost recovery rather than profit maximization.
options.D: DRF drugs are taxed heavily by the federal government.

explanation: Public health revolving funds focus on sustaining stock availability rather than generating financial profit. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T5#GNS215_U3_T5_h1)

question: The baseline procurement expense to land drugs at central medical stores is known as what?
explanation: CIF represents the core purchase and delivery baseline before local distribution costs are added. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T5#GNS215_U3_T5_h2)

question: Why is operational wastage factored into the basic cost components of DRF drugs?

options.A: To increase the salary of the facility pharmacy staff
options.B: To fund community outreach programs by nurses
options.C: To cover potential losses from expired or damaged medications
options.D: To pay taxes to the local government council

explanation: Accounting for stock loss prevents the revolving fund from losing capital due to spoilage or expiration. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T5#GNS215_U3_T5_h2)

question: What determines the percentage mark-up applied to DRF drugs in public facilities?

options.A: Approved institutional or state health policies
options.C: The personal discretion of the dispensing nurse
options.D: The daily market demand at private pharmacies

explanation: Mark-ups are strictly regulated by governing policies to keep essential medicines affordable. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T5#GNS215_U3_T5_h3)

question: A nurse manager adds an excessive, unapproved mark-up to essential antibiotics. What is the most likely consequence?

options.A: Patients will consume fewer drugs and recover much faster.
options.B: The manufacturing companies will lower their wholesale prices.
options.C: Patients will seek care from unregulated and potentially unsafe vendors.
options.D: The Drug Revolving Fund will instantly become a commercial bank.

explanation: Overpricing pushes vulnerable patients away from public facilities into the informal market. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T5#GNS215_U3_T5_h3)

question: What happens to a Drug Revolving Fund when medications are consistently underpriced?

options.A: Increased patronage from wealthy commercial traders
options.B: Elimination of all expired drugs in the warehouse
options.C: Inability to restock due to insufficient capital recovery
options.D: Rapid expansion of hospital pharmacy infrastructure

explanation: Underpricing leads to capital erosion, meaning the facility cannot afford new stock when current supplies run out. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T5#GNS215_U3_T5_h4)

question: The complete absence of essential medicines in a health facility pharmacy is referred to as what?
explanation: Stock-out describes a situation where necessary health commodities are completely unavailable for patients. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T5#GNS215_U3_T5_h4)

question: Why does relying strictly on historical purchase prices cause failure during high inflation?

options.A: The generated revenue will not cover the current higher cost of new stock.
options.B: Suppliers will refuse to deliver drugs in government vehicles.
options.C: Patients will refuse to accept any changes to medication packaging.
options.D: Pharmacy staff will spend more time counting physical inventory.

explanation: If prices do not reflect current replacement costs, sales revenue buys fewer items than before. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T5#GNS215_U3_T5_h5)

question: Which strategy helps buffer a DRF against sudden market shocks and high inflation?

options.A: Bulk procurement and diversified supplier relationships
options.B: Selling all available drugs on credit to community members
options.C: Eliminating all transportation costs from the ledger
options.D: Lowering the retail price below the wholesale purchase rate

explanation: Buying in bulk and having multiple suppliers helps secure better terms and stabilize inventory costs. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T5#GNS215_U3_T5_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of displaying approved price lists visibly in public pharmacies?

options.A: To comply with international nursing uniform codes
options.B: To advertise the hospital to private pharmaceutical investors
options.C: To promote transparency and prevent extortion of patients
options.D: To reduce the workload of the hospital accountant

explanation: Visible pricing reassures patients that they are being charged official, standardized rates. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T5#GNS215_U3_T5_h6)

question: How do regular financial audits protect the long-term survival of a Drug Revolving Fund?

options.A: By increasing the speed at which nurses dispense prescriptions
options.B: By identifying financial leakages and ensuring cash matches dispensed stock
options.C: By setting the clinical diagnosis guidelines for prescribing physicians
options.D: By determining the exact chemical composition of imported tablets

explanation: Audits track financial discrepancies, ensuring revenue generated from drug sales is properly accounted for. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T5#GNS215_U3_T5_h6)
